mula_devanagari: सर्वेन्द्रिय-गुणाभासं सर्वेन्द्रिय-विवर्जितम् | असक्तं सर्व-भृच् चैव निर्गुणं गुण-भोक्तृ च
mula_iast: sarvendriya-guṇābhāsaṃ sarvendriya-vivarjitam | asaktaṃ sarva-bhṛc caiva nirguṇaṃ guṇa-bhoktṛ ca
jayatirtha_prameyadipika: ।।13.15।।अहं परा शक्तिर्यस्येति व्याख्यानेऽर्थासम्भवं कश्चिदन्यथा प्राह -- ब्रह्मणः सर्वविशेषप्रतिषेधेनैवात्र तदविजिज्ञापयिषितत्वात्। शक्तिमत्त्वप्रतिपादनं विरुद्धम् इति। तदसत्? अत्र विशेषवत्त्वस्य दर्शनादिति भावेनाह -- सर्वे ति। गुणांस्तद्विषयानाभासयति प्रत्याययति प्रत्येतीति वा। भासतेः पचाद्यत्। एवंसर्वतःपाणिपादं तत् [13।14]सर्वभृत् गुणभोक्तृ च इत्यादिकमप्युदाहार्यम्। कथं तर्हि सर्वेन्द्रियविवर्जितं निर्गुणमचरमित्याद्युक्तमित्यत आह -- इन्द्रिये ति। आदिशब्दात्परं शब्देत्यध्याहार्यम्। पुरस्तात् द्वितीये।

current_dvaita_rendering.english: [Very thin bhāṣya.] It makes all the senses and the guṇa (qualities) shine forth; hence it is 'sarvendriya-guṇābhāsa'. The meaning of 'devoid of senses' and the rest was stated earlier.
current_dvaita_rendering.divergence_note: THIN: Madhva's entire supplied comment is two sentences. Its one doctrinal move is to read ābhāsa causatively (ābhāsayati: it illumines), so the Lord is the illuminer of senses and guṇa, not one who merely appears through them. For the remaining terms he refers back to an earlier passage not supplied here; nothing more is rendered.

current_dvaita_everyday: Madhva's brief note makes the knower the one who lights up the senses, not a passenger inside them. Before trusting a report, a dashboard or your own eyes, ask what is making that information visible to you at all. His note is too short to support more than this.

other_schools_english.advaita: It shines through the functions of all the senses and of buddhi (intellect) and manas (mind), deciding, willing, hearing, speaking, so that knowable seems busy with their work, as the Śruti says 'it seems to meditate, it seems to move'; but it is devoid of all organs, so it is not truly busy, and 'without hands and feet he speeds' shows only its power to conform to the adjuncts, not literal motion. Being without organs it is asakta (free of all contact), and yet it bears all, for everything rests on sat (being), as even a mirage is not without a ground. Free of the three guṇa (qualities), it is yet their bhoktṛ (experiencer), the witness of sattva, rajas and tamas as they turn, through sound and the rest, into pleasure, pain and delusion.
other_schools_english.viśiṣṭādvaita: Its manifestation comes by way of the functions of all the senses: it is able to know objects even through sense-activity, yet by its own nature it is devoid of the senses and knows everything by itself, without them. By nature unattached to divine, human and other bodies, it is still able to sustain all those bodies, as the Śruti says 'he becomes one, he becomes three'. By nature free of sattva and the other guṇa (qualities), it is able to enjoy them.
other_schools_english.śuddhādvaita: [Thin for this verse.] The purpose of its delimitation everywhere has already been explained at 'ananta' (11.47) and 'avyakta' (13.6); by this its doing the work of eye and the rest everywhere is stated, for the Śruti 'without hands and feet he speeds and grasps, sees without eyes, hears without ears' first denies prākṛta (material) organs and then speaks of aprākṛta (non-material) ones. Now, with 'sarvendriya-guṇābhāsam', He declares that He is the seat of viruddha-dharma (contradictory attributes).
other_schools_english.bhakti: It shines in the form of the modes of the eye and the other senses, as form and the rest; or, it makes the senses and their objects shine. It is devoid of all senses, as the Śruti says 'without hands and feet he speeds', and asakta (without attachment), yet it bears all, being the support of all. That very one is nirguṇa (free of sattva and the other qualities), and yet the bhoktṛ of the guṇa, which here means their pālaka (protector).
other_schools_english.advaita-bhakti: Having explained the supreme Brahman by adhyāropa (superimposing the whole world on it), following the maxim 'by superimposition and rescission the world-free is set forth', the Lord now begins the apavāda (rescission) to teach its unconditioned nature. In truth it is devoid of all senses; by māyā (illusory power) it shines as if through their functions, deciding, willing, hearing, speaking, as if busy, and in truth it is unattached, yet it bears and nourishes all that is imagined in it as their being, since an error without a substrate is impossible. In truth nirguṇa (beyond sattva, rajas and tamas), it is the bhoktṛ, the perceiver of the guṇa as they change through sound and the rest into pleasure, pain and delusion.
